561: A is correct because DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, in-memory cache purpose-built for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond response times for reads with minimal configuration. DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB, so the application only needs to route reads through the DAX endpoint rather than implementing custom caching or invalidation logic. This gives the lowest operational overhead compared to self-managed ElastiCache or Lambda-based cache population, which require you to build and maintain synchronization code.
562: A and B are correct because a DynamoDB gateway endpoint is accessed through route table entries, so creating the gateway endpoint and adding a route to it in the VPC route tables keeps traffic on the AWS private network. B is correct because the gateway endpoint for DynamoDB is the supported VPC endpoint type that lets EC2 instances reach DynamoDB without traversing the internet. A is correct because gateway endpoints are enabled per subnet by adding a route to the endpoint's prefix list, unlike interface endpoints which require ENIs and security groups.
563: B is correct because Amazon EKS Connector is the AWS feature designed to register external Kubernetes clusters, including on-premises clusters, so they can be viewed and managed from the Amazon EKS console alongside EKS clusters. This gives a single central location for all clusters and workloads with no agents or infrastructure to operate. Monitoring-based approaches only collect metrics rather than providing a unified view of the clusters themselves.
564: B is correct because AWS KMS client-side encryption encrypts sensitive data in the application before it is ever sent to the RDS database, so the plaintext is never exposed to the database layer or its administrators. Even a database administrator with full access to the RDS instance only sees ciphertext, because decryption requires KMS keys with policies that the administrators do not control. Server-side or storage-level encryption options do not protect data from administrators who can query the database itself.
565: C is correct because AWS DMS is the managed migration service that can move an on-premises MySQL database to Amazon Aurora with minimal effort, and Aurora is MySQL-compatible so existing applications continue to work without changes. Aurora Auto Scaling automatically adds and removes Aurora Replicas to handle increased demand. Redshift is an analytics data warehouse and DynamoDB is a NoSQL database, both of which would break compatibility, and RDS for MySQL does not offer the same automatic read scaling.
566: B is correct because Amazon EFS is a managed shared file system that supports the Network File System protocol, provides a hierarchical directory structure, and can be mounted concurrently by multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones with low latency. EFS supports concurrent reads and writes from many instances, which is exactly the shared storage requirement. EBS volumes cannot be attached to multiple instances for shared read/write access, and S3 is object storage without a file system interface.
567: A is correct because API Gateway with Lambda and DynamoDB is a fully serverless, managed architecture that receives HTTP requests from the sensors, processes them, and stores the data without any servers to patch or scale. Serverless components are independently extendable, which suits the plan to add independent features later. The EC2 and Elastic Load Balancer options require managing instances, and SQL Server Express on EC2 is unmanaged, adding significant operational overhead.
568: A is correct because Amazon S3 provides virtually unlimited object storage that can scale to petabytes of data for the engineering drawings at low cost. Amazon CloudFront is a CDN that caches the drawings at edge locations close to users, minimizing load times. Glacier is archival storage with high retrieval delays, EBS cannot scale to petabytes as shared storage, and Storage Gateway is a hybrid cache for on-premises access rather than a caching layer for web users.
569: A is correct because Amazon EventBridge publishes operational metrics to Amazon CloudWatch in the AWS/Events namespace, including metrics such as TriggeredRules, Invocations, and FailedInvocations. These metrics let you confirm whether the rule matched events and whether the target was invoked, which directly answers both questions. CloudTrail records management API calls rather than rule evaluation, and the other options are not where EventBridge rule invocation data appears by default.
570: B is correct because an Auto Scaling group with a scheduled action can automatically scale out to six instances every Friday evening and scale back to two, handling a predictable recurring workload with no manual intervention. This is the least overhead solution because scheduling is set once and repeats automatically. Manual scaling requires weekly intervention, automatic scaling reacts to metrics rather than the known schedule, and an EventBridge reminder still requires a human to act.
571: A is correct because certificates from a specific third-party public CA must be created outside AWS and imported into ACM, since ACM cannot issue certificates through an arbitrary external CA. ACM only issues certificates through its own trusted CA partners, so the only way to use a specific third-party CA's certificate is to obtain it on a local machine and import it. An API Gateway custom domain with an HTTP API can then use the imported ACM certificate, and the HTTP API supports the required TLSv1.3, whereas Lambda function URLs cannot be configured with custom certificates.
572: C is correct because Aurora Serverless v2 is a MySQL-compatible managed database that automatically and continuously scales capacity in ACUs based on demand, with a minimum capacity of as low as 0.5 or 1 ACU. Setting a 1 ACU minimum matches the consistent baseline usage while still allowing automatic scaling for unexpected workload increases, all with virtually no administrative overhead. Provisioned Aurora or RDS cannot automatically scale compute, and DynamoDB is not MySQL-compatible.
573: D is correct because Lambda SnapStart improves startup performance for functions running on Java 11 and later managed runtimes by initializing the function once, snapshotting the memory and execution environment, and reusing that snapshot for subsequent invocations. This significantly reduces cold starts and outlier latencies during scale-up at no additional cost, only a storage fee for snapshots. Provisioned concurrency also reduces cold starts but incurs continuous hourly charges, making it less cost-effective given the relaxed latency requirements.
574: A is correct because Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity automatically in fine-grained increments and bills only for the ACUs consumed per second, so a database used only two hours per week costs almost nothing the rest of the time. Since the workload runs briefly each week, Aurora Serverless v2 eliminates paying for continuously provisioned instances. Provisioned Aurora clusters, EC2 reservations, and ECS tasks all incur costs or management overhead even when the database is idle.
575: C is correct because an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster for PostgreSQL provides a primary with two readable standby instances across three Availability Zones, delivering both high availability through automatic failover and increased read capacity by serving reads from the standbys. This is the most operationally efficient way to get HA plus read scaling in a single managed PostgreSQL deployment. A standard Multi-AZ deployment has a standby that cannot serve reads, and cross-Region read replicas add cost and complexity without improving local HA.
576: D is correct because an edge-optimized endpoint routes API requests through Amazon CloudFront edge locations, so geographically distributed users connect to the nearest edge point of presence, reducing latency. Regional endpoints serve traffic from a single Region, and private or interface VPC endpoints are intended for private access from within a VPC rather than for public globally distributed users.
577: C is correct because AWS Certificate Manager issues certificates and handles automatic renewal, and DNS validation is the most operationally efficient validation method because once the DNS CNAME record is in place, validation and all future renewals happen automatically without human action. Email validation requires responding to emails, which can be missed and disrupts automation. ACM is the native service for provisioning and renewing CloudFront certificates, as CloudFront policies and OAC do not create certificates.
578: A is correct because DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed in-memory cache for DynamoDB that improves read response times from milliseconds to microseconds. DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB, so enabling it requires minimal application changes and no cache management infrastructure, providing the least operational overhead. ElastiCache for Redis would require managing cache invalidation and consistency logic, while migrating to Redshift or RDS changes the database engine entirely.
579: A is correct because the Instance Scheduler on AWS is a pre-built AWS Solutions implementation designed to start and stop EC2 and RDS instances on configured schedules, matching weekday business hours usage with no custom code. This automatically reduces costs during nights and weekends while the database remains fully managed. Custom Lambda functions add development and maintenance overhead, disabling backups sacrifices durability, and reserved instances provide no savings when usage is only part-time.
580: D is correct because a lift and shift of a latency-sensitive application on locally attached storage maps most directly and cost-effectively to a single EC2 instance with an attached EBS volume, and gp3 volumes deliver high performance at a lower price per GB than gp2 with a higher baseline of 3,000 IOPS. Since the application runs on one server on premises, no Auto Scaling group or shared file system is needed. FSx file systems add unnecessary cost and architecture changes for a single-instance workload.
